items.prompt: Delete every node from a linked list whose value appears more than once, keeping only values that were unique. The list is sorted.
items.why: Deleting runs of nodes, possibly including the head → dummy head + prev/curr unlinking. There are no two speeds and no reversal.

items.prompt: Return the middle node of a linked list in a single pass.
items.why: 'Middle in one pass' → slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle.

items.prompt: Rearrange a list so all nodes with value < x come before nodes with value ≥ x, keeping the original relative order within each group.
items.why: Stable split into groups → build two lists with two dummy heads and join them. No reversing involved.

items.prompt: Reverse the nodes of a linked list k at a time, leaving a final group of fewer than k nodes as it is.
items.why: 'Reverse' groups in place → prev/curr/nxt reversal per group. A stack would work but costs O(k) extra space.

items.prompt: Two numbers are stored as linked lists of digits in reverse order. Return their sum as a linked list.
items.why: Walk both lists in lock-step with a carry, building the output behind a dummy. The digits are already least-significant first, so there's no need to reverse.

items.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
items.why: k sorted inputs → a min-heap of the k current heads gives O(N log k). Pairwise merging one after another is O(N·k).

items.prompt: Design a cache with get and put in O(1) that evicts the least recently used key when it's full.
items.why: O(1) 'move to front' and 'remove the oldest' → a doubly linked list (plus a hash map from key to node). A heap makes each operation O(log n). A stack can't remove from the bottom.

items.prompt: Determine whether a linked list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra memory.
items.why: A visited set works but uses O(n) memory; with O(1) memory, a fast pointer catches up with the slow one inside a cycle.
